s: A. Judicial review of state and federal action.
Section 25 of the Judiciary Act of 1789 gave the Supreme Court appellate jurisdiction over state high courts that rejected federal claims.
Martin v. Hunter's Lessee (1816) upheld that review of state courts in civil cases, and Cohens v. Virginia (1821) extended it to criminal cases.
The Court reasoned that national uniformity in federal law requires a single final interpreter.
The Court reviews only federal questions.

If a state-court judgment rests on a state-law ground that is adequate (it alone supports the judgment) and independent (not intertwined with federal law), the Court will not review it, because any federal ruling would be advisory.
When a state opinion is ambiguous, Michigan v. Long (1983) presumes the decision rests on federal law unless the state court makes a "plain statement" that state law independently supports it.
Does the judgment rest on a state-law ground that would sustain it regardless of the federal issue?
Is that ground free of reliance on federal law?
If the opinion is ambiguous, presume federal reliance unless there is a clear statement otherwise (Michigan v. Long).
